# Staff System

**Last updated:** 9 September 2026
**Register item:** A8
**Status:** Batch A is closed. The capacity and crew tables are generated by `tools/balance/model.py`.

---

## Why it matters

In the research, the most praised side of Tavern Keeper was that the staff had character. Cat Cafe Manager, on the other hand, sank because of the stupidity of its staff AI and the feeling that "skills do not matter".

Two lessons: **staff must have character, and their skills must really make a difference.**

---

## The four roles

| Role | Job | Daily wage | Stations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook | Cooks the food | 140 | Stove, grill, oven |
| Waiter | Takes orders, serves | 110 | Hall |
| Cashier | Takes payment | 100 | Till |
| Dishwasher | The plate cycle, cleaning | 90 | Dishwashing |

The roles are common to every cuisine. What changes is the station types.

**Why the dishwasher exists:** if the plates run out, service stops. An invisible bottleneck that is only noticed once it blocks. It teaches the player "do not neglect the thing that looks unimportant".

---

## Twelve traits

Every staff member draws **two traits** from the pool. Conflicting traits never come together.

| Trait | Effect |
|---|---|
| Fast but Messy | Speed +18%, cleanliness -15% |
| Slow but Careful | Speed -12%, food quality +20% |
| Panics in a Rush | Speed -25% in busy slices |
| Unflappable | No busyness penalty |
| Good with People | Satisfaction +8 at the table they serve |
| Surly | Satisfaction -6 at the table they serve |
| Tires Quickly | Speed -20% in the last quarter of the day |
| Tireless | No tiring |
| Lifts the Team | Other staff's morale +10 |
| Bad-Tempered | Other staff's morale -8 |
| Apprentice | Wage -25%, speed -15%, double experience gain |
| Experienced | Wage +30%, speed +15%, gains no experience |

**The conflicts:** Fast but Messy with Slow but Careful, Panics in a Rush with Unflappable, Tires Quickly with Tireless, Good with People with Surly, Lifts the Team with Bad-Tempered, Apprentice with Experienced.

**Design intent:** no trait is purely good or purely bad. The apprentice is cheap but slow, the experienced one is fast but expensive. The right trait depends on the right station. Someone who panics in a rush is a disaster on the till and no problem at the sink.

---

## Morale

Between 0 and 100. New staff start at 70.

| Event | Change |
|---|---|
| Wages paid on time | +5 |
| Wages late | -25 |
| Busy days back to back | -3 per day |
| A day off was given | +10 |
| A raise was given | +15 |
| Someone who lifts the team is present | +10 |
| Someone bad-tempered is present | -8 |
| The end-of-year evaluation went well | +20 |

### Morale thresholds

| Morale | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Above 70 | Working normally |
| 30-70 | No speed loss, but the chance of a mistake rises slightly |
| Below 30 | Speed -20%, the chance of a mistake rises noticeably |
| Below 15 | A 10% chance of resigning every day |

**The connection to the bankruptcy ladder:** a late wage is the third rung of the ladder. The collapse of morale and a resignation become the concrete face of going under. Losing a number is abstract; an employee whose name you know handing in their notice is concrete.

---

## Experience and levels

- **1 experience point** for every day worked. 2 if they have the apprentice trait.
- **They level up at 30 points.** Maximum 3 levels.
- Every level brings speed +10%.
- On levelling up, **the wage demand goes up 15%**. If you refuse, morale -20.

This gives the player a real decision: keeping a good worker gets more expensive. Take on somebody new and cheap and train them from scratch, or give the raise and carry on?

---

## Hiring

- **Three candidates** appear on the hiring screen at once.
- Candidates are generated: role, two traits, appearance, name.
- The candidate pool refreshes **every three days**. You can reject a candidate you do not like, but a new one does not arrive immediately.
- There is no hiring fee. Only the wage.
- A candidate's traits are **visible before you hire them.** No hidden information, because this is a management game, not a gamble.

### How many people you can employ

| Tables | Maximum staff |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2 |
| 7 | 4 |
| 10 | 6 |
| 14 | 8 |

The limit depends on the venue tier. There is no point hiring a lot of staff into a small restaurant; they do not fit anyway.

---

## Firing

- Severance: **one week's wage.**
- The person dismissed leaves that day.
- The other staff's morale drops **-10**. When somebody leaves the crew, everyone is affected.

Severance and the morale penalty together make "throw out the one you do not like and hire another" expensive.

---

## Station assignment

Every morning, in the counter phase, you distribute the staff across the stations.

- More than one person can work at a station, but the return diminishes. The second person contributes 70%, the third 45%.
- A staff member assigned to a station outside their role works at **50% efficiency**. A waiter can move to the stove, but it will not go well.
- The assignment cannot be changed during the day. The decision you make in the morning determines the day.

**That last rule is important.** If stations could be changed during service, the morning decision would lose its meaning. The game's main idea is the correctness of the preparation.

---

## The capacity model: how many staff for how many customers

This section is the heart of the game's growth pressure. When the restaurant grows, customers increase; when customers increase, staff are needed; when staff increase, wages increase.

### Daily capacity

Every role has a daily capacity. The base values, for a level-one, bad-tempered staff member:

<!-- GENERATED: capacity -->
| Role | Daily capacity | Daily wage | Work per guest | Share of hall load |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cook | 28 guests | 140 | 0.0357 person-days | separate pool |
| Waiter | 26 guests | 110 | 0.0385 person-days | 52% |
| Dishwasher | 48 guests | 90 | 0.0208 person-days | 28% |
| Cashier | 70 guests | 100 | 0.0143 person-days | 19% |
<!-- /GENERATED: capacity -->

**The waiter is the first place to block.** They carry 52 per cent of the hall's workload. That is deliberate: the first bottleneck the player notices should be in the hall, because that is where it is visible.

### Two pools, one owner

The review found that the old model counted the owner in three columns at once. The corrected model uses two pools:

**The cook pool.** Calculated separately. The owner cannot cook — the player is the owner, not the chef. Cooks needed = peak customers ÷ 28, rounded up.

**The hall pool.** Waiter, dishwasher and cashier are a single work pool. In a small lokanta the same person serves, watches the till and clears the plates. The capacity calculation is not done per station but in **person-days**:

```
hall_workload = peak_customers × 0.0769 person-days
hall_needed   = ceiling(hall_workload − owner_contribution)
```

The station assignment is visible to the player and affects performance, but the size of the crew is determined by the workload. This removes the absurdity of "0.4 of a waiter".

### The owner's contribution

The player works too. The owner contributes **1.4 person-days** in the hall, that is, more than one member of staff. Because it is their own business they take on more.

**But they can only be in one place at a time.** That was the old model's bug: when the owner was counted in three columns at once, one person was providing capacity for 36 customers.

This contribution is enough to get through the first week with a single cook: the hall load of a 17-customer peak is 1.31 person-days and the owner carries 1.4. In the second week it rises to 1.46 and the first waiter is needed. **The game's first hire comes from here, not from a script.**

### How capacity grows

| Source | Effect |
|---|---|
| Experience level | +10% per level, at most +30% |
| Traits | Fast but Messy +18%, apprentice −15%, and so on |
| Equipment | Increases the station count, raises the cook ceiling |

### The crew needed

<!-- GENERATED: crew -->
| Week | Peak guests/day | Cooks | Hall | Total crew | Cap | Hall workload | After the owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 17 | 1 | 0 | **1** | 3 | 1.25 | 0.00 |
| 2 | 19 | 1 | 1 | **2** | 3 | 1.40 | 0.10 |
| 3 | 36 | 2 | 2 | **4** | 5 | 2.65 | 1.35 |
| 4 | 39 | 2 | 2 | **4** | 5 | 2.87 | 1.57 |
| 5 | 59 | 3 | 4 | **7** | 8 | 4.34 | 3.04 |
| 6 | 63 | 3 | 4 | **7** | 8 | 4.64 | 3.34 |
| 7 | 92 | 4 | 6 | **10** | 12 | 6.77 | 5.47 |
| 8 | 97 | 4 | 6 | **10** | 12 | 7.14 | 5.84 |
<!-- /GENERATED: crew -->

The crew is set to the **weekend peak**, and its wage is paid for seven days. A restaurant that cannot cover the peak loses reputation; an oversized crew pays wages for empty days.

Because the wage demand rises as experience is gained, a cumulative 2.2% weekly raise is applied. By the eighth week that adds roughly 16% on top of the base wage.

### The crew cap

| Tables | Cap | Maximum needed at that tier | Slack |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
| 7 | 5 | 4 | 1 |
| 10 | 8 | 7 | 1 |
| 14 | 12 | 11 | 1 |

**The cap is one above what is needed at every tier.** The player has room for error but cannot inflate the crew. An extra person hired is written straight to the loss.

---

## The penalty for an understaffed crew

If the capacity is not enough the game does not hand out a penalty, **it punishes itself.** The loop is this:

1. There are not enough staff
2. Waiting times get longer
3. Patience runs out, customers walk out
4. Satisfaction falls
5. Reputation falls
6. Fewer customers come the next day

The sixth step matters: an understaffed crew hits tomorrow too. It is not a one-day mistake, it is a collapse that feeds itself.

**The penalty for an oversized crew** is simpler: wages are paid whether customers come or not. Hiring three people into a four-table restaurant is a straight loss.

The two penalties together make the crew decision a real decision. Neither too few nor too many.

---

## The economics of growth

Growing the restaurant does three things at once:

| Effect | Direction |
|---|---|
| More tables, more customers | Revenue rises |
| More customers, more staff | Wages rise |
| A bigger venue | Rent rises |

The result is that the profit margin improves **slowly**.

<!-- GENERATED: margin -->
| Week | Stock | Wages | Rent | Expansion | Net margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 32% | 27% | 23% | 0% | **17.7%** |
| 2 | 32% | 42% | 21% | 0% | **5.2%** |
| 3 | 32% | 42% | 23% | 29% | **−26.0%** |
| 4 | 32% | 38% | 21% | 0% | **9.1%** |
| 5 | 32% | 41% | 19% | 29% | **−20.2%** |
| 6 | 32% | 37% | 17% | 0% | **14.0%** |
| 7 | 32% | 35% | 18% | 29% | **−14.4%** |
| 8 | 32% | 31% | 16% | 0% | **20.1%** |
<!-- /GENERATED: margin -->

**All three expansion weeks go negative.** The rent and the crew grow at the same time while the reputation has not caught up. This is deliberate and was written into the model as a constraint.

In the eighth week the net margin reaches 20 per cent. Growing pays, but by a factor of two, not eleven. This curve is what protects us from the "more money than you can spend" trap in the research.

**The wage share falls, and so does the rent share.** From 30 per cent to 24, from 33 per cent to 24. Economies of scale work, but slowly. The improving margin is the reward for growth.

**The average ticket grows too:** 50 in the first week, 75 in the eighth. As the menu widens, expensive dishes open and mechanics like the combo come into play. This is a hidden growth lever.

---

## Three named staff

Three staff members per cuisine are hand-designed. They get a name, a face, traits and a small story.

- These appear in the candidate pool on specific days, **guaranteed**.
- Their traits are fixed, not random.
- They have their own story beats: why they are looking for this job, what they want to do.
- If they are kept on for a long time, extra scenes open.

Generated staff also have a name and traits, so nobody is nameless. The difference is whether there is a hand-written story.

---

## Staff AI: it will be kept simple

This was the shared wound of Cat Cafe Manager and Tavern Keeper. Workers who cannot find their way, standing around idle.

**Decision: no complex pathfinding.**

- Staff are fixed to their station; they do not wander the hall.
- The waiter goes to the table, but the route is precomputed, short and predictable.
- The queue logic is simple: the table that has waited longest goes first.
- No collision; staff can pass through each other. It is not noticeable visually and it removes a whole class of bug.

A simple system that works correctly is better than a complex one that works badly. The player does not notice the pathfinding algorithm, but they notice a stuck worker immediately.

## Details awaiting a decision

1. Should the maximum level stay at three
2. Should the candidate pool refresh every three days
3. Will there be a day-off mechanic, or should morale depend only on wages
4. Should staff tiredness be visible during the day

**Closed questions.** "Is a waiter capacity of 16 right" and "is the owner's 12-customer contribution reasonable" were closed in Batch A. The capacities are 28/25/46/66 and the owner's contribution is 1.4 person-days. Neither is a guess; both were searched for from the design targets by `tools/balance/solve.py`.
